passage: The water tanker reached the village square at noon, and within minutes the line of pots had broken into a shoving crowd. Hafsa, sixteen, stood with her cousin Sharmila holding two steel matkas. A man from the big house pushed his pots to the front. "Everyone knows Abba's family never cut a line," Hafsa said quietly, remembering how people still spoke of her grandfather, the old sarpanch who'd refused bribes. She set her pots down at the back. Then, instead of arguing, she began arranging the pots in a row, calling out, "Old people and pregnant women first." A few women laughed but joined in. The man hesitated, embarrassed, and moved his pots. Sharmila whispered, "Your Abba would be proud." Hafsa didn't answer, but she stood a little straighter.

qa.q: Who did Hafsa say should get water first?
qa.a: Old people and pregnant women.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa stand a little straighter when Sharmila spoke?
qa.a: She felt proud and connected to her grandfather's honest name, and pleased that her own actions kept that reputation alive.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than arguing with the man, and why?
qa.a: Organising a fair line gave everyone a clear rule to follow, so the man could step back without a fight.

qa.q: How might the other women see Hafsa after this?
qa.a: They may admire her for bringing order and fairness to the square, and link her behaviour to her family's good name.

grounding: Shows a teen upholding fair civic order in her village while honouring the family reputation she admires.

passage: Mateo and Oskar were walking home through the old square of their town near Valencia when Oskar pulled a spray can from his backpack. "The town hall wall, right there. Just our tag. Nobody's watching." Mateo's stomach tightened. His grandmother had sat on the town council for twelve years, and people still stopped her in the market to thank her for the new park. He pictured her face if she heard. "It's not ours to spray, man," he said. "And it's a fine for your parents if the cameras catch you." Oskar rolled his eyes. "You sound like a politician." Mateo laughed, but he didn't move. "There's a youth council meeting on Thursday. They want ideas for a legal graffiti wall. Come with me." Oskar shoved the can back into his bag.

qa.q: When was the youth council meeting?
qa.a: On Thursday.

qa.q: What did Mateo picture that made his stomach tighten?
qa.a: He pictured his grandmother's face, and he seemed worried about hurting her and the respect her work on the council had earned.

qa.q: What made Mateo's suggestion a good way forward?
qa.a: He did not just say no; he gave Oskar a lawful place to use his creativity, which respects the town and keeps his friend.

qa.q: How does Oskar see Mateo's stance at first?
qa.a: He thinks Mateo is being stiff and rule-bound, which is why he teases that he sounds like a politician.

grounding: A teen abroad refuses to deface public property, drawing on respect for civic rules and his family's standing.

passage: The school's mock parliament met in the assembly hall every Friday, and this term Chetan had been chosen as Speaker. He'd spent the week reading how real sessions ran: who could speak, for how long, how a bill was passed. Halfway through the debate on a plastic ban, his best friend Sumit jumped up and interrupted the opposition leader for the third time. The hall giggled. Chetan's ears burned. Everyone knew they sat together at lunch. "Honourable member," he said, voice shaking only slightly, "please wait for your turn, or I'll have to ask you to leave the house." Sumit stared, then sat down. Later, at the tap outside, Sumit bumped his shoulder. "Strict, huh." "Rules are the same for everyone," Chetan said. "Otherwise what's the point?"

qa.q: What was the mock parliament debating when Sumit interrupted?
qa.a: A plastic ban.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he had to warn Sumit?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and nervous, with burning ears and a slightly shaky voice, because enforcing rules on his best friend felt risky.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on what happened in the session?
qa.a: The teacher could praise the fair handling in front of the class and discuss why rules only work when applied equally.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit to be warned by his friend in front of everyone?
qa.a: It probably stings at first, but his shoulder bump afterward suggests he respects Chetan and is not holding a grudge.

grounding: Shows a teen in a school mock parliament learning how governance works and applying rules fairly even to a friend.

passage:
Dear Nandini,
Big week here. On Tuesday I found a wallet near the bus stop with four thousand rupees and a driving licence in it. My first thought, honestly, was that I could buy those headphones. Then I thought of Dadaji; everyone in our lane calls him 'the man who never kept a paisa that wasn't his.' I didn't want to be the one who broke that. So Papa and I took it to the police station. I was nervous, but the constable was kind. He showed me the register where they log found property and explained that the owner has to show ID to claim it. The owner, an old tailor, called on Thursday and cried on the phone. Dadaji didn't say much. He just put his hand on my head at dinner.
Miss you,
Hansa

qa.q: How much money was in the wallet?
qa.a: Four thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Hansa think of Dadaji when finding the wallet?
qa.a: Hansa valued the family name for honesty that Dadaji built and didn't want to be the one to break it.

qa.q: What did Hansa's family get right in how they handled the wallet?
qa.a: Papa went with Hansa to the police station, so Hansa learned the proper legal process instead of handling it alone.

qa.q: How might the tailor have felt when getting the call?
qa.a: Deeply relieved and grateful, which is why the tailor cried on the phone.

grounding: Shows a teenager acting to uphold the family's good name and following the lawful process for found property.

passage: 'Jeevan, you'll laugh, but the most interesting thing I did this holiday was stand in a queue at the municipal office. Papa had to pay the house tax, and he made me come. I was sulking. Then the clerk showed me the receipt, and there was this line: part of it goes to the ward's water and drains. I asked him, so if people don't pay, the drains near our school just stay broken? He said, "More or less." That stuck with me. Now I notice things, the new streetlight, the park gate. I read the ward notice board for the first time. Papa told me, "Yash, my father used to say paying on time is part of our family's respect." I used to think that was just old talk.'

qa.q: Where did Yash stand in a queue?
qa.a: At the municipal office.

qa.q: What does 'That stuck with me' suggest about how Yash's thinking changed?
qa.a: Yash began to see taxes as tied to things Yash uses, like drains and streetlights, instead of a boring chore.

qa.q: What could Yash do next to act on this new interest?
qa.a: Yash could keep reading the ward notice board or attend a ward meeting with Papa to see how decisions are made.

qa.q: How might Papa feel hearing Yash talk this way?
qa.a: Probably pleased, since Papa made Yash come along and the family value is finally making sense to Yash. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teenager starting to understand civic duties like taxes and linking them to family respect.

passage: I'm Damini, from the flat across the corridor. Chandrika, who's seventeen, stopped her cousin at the gate last Sunday. He was about to ride off on the scooter without a helmet. "It's the law, and you know Papa's rule: nobody from our house gets a challan," she said, holding out the helmet. He rolled his eyes but wore it. She also volunteers with the colony's traffic awareness drive and reads the rules out loud to anyone who'll listen. I can't tell if it's pride or worry, but she clearly cares what her family's name stands for.

qa.q: What did Chandrika hold out to her cousin?
qa.a: The helmet.

qa.q: What might Chandrika have felt when her cousin rolled his eyes?
qa.a: Probably a little annoyed, but firm and protective, caring more about his safety than his mood.

qa.q: What would you advise Chandrika to keep her message from sounding preachy?
qa.a: Explain the reasons calmly and set an example, rather than lecturing everyone she meets.

qa.q: How does Damini see Chandrika's actions?
qa.a: Damini notices real care for the law and family name, though unsure whether it's pride or worry.

grounding: Shows a teenager respecting traffic law and her family's standards, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday: Asif, sixteen, found a phone on the bus seat, locked, battery low. His friend said, "Keep it." Asif took it home. Tuesday: his uncle Tanvir said, "You don't keep what isn't yours. Take it to the police station." Asif was nervous; he'd never been inside one. Wednesday: the constable at the desk wrote down his name, logged the phone and thanked him. "Most people don't bother." A week later, the owner, an old schoolteacher, called to thank him. Asif told Tanvir, "I thought police stations were scary. They were just… doing their job."

qa.q: Who was the phone's owner?
qa.a: An old schoolteacher.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling about going to the police station?
qa.a: He felt nervous, never having been inside one before.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do that helped Asif act rightly?
qa.a: He made clear that keeping it was wrong and pointed to the proper place to hand it in.

qa.q: How might the constable see Asif handing in the phone?
qa.a: With appreciation, since most people don't bother.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to trust public institutions by doing his civic duty with a lost phone.

passage: "Devika, you think voting is a small thing? When I, your Disha Nani, was seventeen, too young to vote, my father was a polling officer in our village. He took me along to carry the ink and the forms. I watched an old woman walk three kilometres, barefoot, to put her mark on a paper. My father treated her like the most important person in the room. Afterwards he said, 'Our family's honour is not our land. It's doing this job properly.' The next year, on my first vote, I wore my best sari."

qa.q: What did young Disha carry to the polling booth?
qa.a: The ink and the forms.

qa.q: What was young Disha feeling as she watched the old woman vote?
qa.a: She felt moved and full of admiration for the woman's effort and her father's respect.

qa.q: What turning point in the story shaped Disha's sense of civic duty?
qa.a: Seeing her father treat the old woman with respect and hearing what family honour meant to him.

qa.q: How might the old woman have felt being treated so respectfully?
qa.a: Valued and proud that her vote mattered.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager she learned civic duty and a sense of family honour at a polling booth.

passage: It was forty degrees outside the polling booth in Jaipur, and the line wrapped around the school. Rashmi, seventeen, held an umbrella over Himani Nani, who had insisted on voting "as I have since 1971." At the front, the officer shook his head. "The voter slip isn't enough, Mataji. I need your ID." Nani's face fell. Rashmi's first thought was to beg him to let it go. Then she thought: rules are rules, even for Nani. "I'll run home and get it," she said. "Ten minutes." She ran through the heat, found the card in Nani's steel trunk, and ran back. When Nani came out with ink on her finger, she held it up proudly. Rashmi felt oddly proud too, though she was too young to vote.

qa.q: What did the officer need from Himani Nani?
qa.a: Her ID.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Nani came out with ink on her finger?
qa.a: She felt proud and moved, respecting both her grandmother and the vote, though too young to vote herself.

qa.q: Which choice was wiser, and why?
qa.a: Running home for the ID instead of begging the officer, because it respected the rule and still got Nani her vote.

qa.q: How might Himani Nani feel about Rashmi running home for the ID?
qa.a: She likely felt grateful and proud of her granddaughter.

grounding: A teenager helps her grandmother vote in the heat, respecting the polling rules and civic duty.

passage: Late one night in Kalyan, Kunal's friend Thomas pulled a spray can from his bag. "The new wall by the railway bridge. Our names, big." Kunal's stomach dropped. He'd seen the municipal notice: fines for defacing public walls. And his father was on the colony committee; everyone knew the family. "It's not our wall," Kunal said. "Relax, nobody's watching." "That's not the point." Thomas sulked. Kunal thought for a minute. "Let's ask the committee if we can paint the old compound wall. A proper mural." Two weeks later, with permission, they painted a huge tiger on it. Kunal's father walked past, stopped, and grinned. People took photos. Thomas signed his name, small, in the corner, and admitted it was better.

qa.q: What did they paint on the compound wall?
qa.a: A huge tiger.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when Thomas pulled out the spray can?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and worried, about the law and about his family's name.

qa.q: What alternative did Kunal suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking the committee for permission to paint a mural, which kept the fun but respected the rules.

qa.q: How might Kunal's father feel seeing the mural?
qa.a: He was clearly pleased and proud of his son's idea.

grounding: A teenager refuses to deface a public wall, thinking of the law and his family's name, and proposes a permitted mural.

passage:
"Mumma, Rohit drives his dad's car. Why can't I?"
"Ojas, you're sixteen."
"I know how. Papa showed me in the parking lot."
"In the parking lot. The law says eighteen, with a licence."
"Rohit's parents don't care."
"And if he hits someone?" Chandrika put down her cup. "Who pays? Who carries that?"
Ojas shrugged. "Nothing will happen."
"That's what everyone says before something happens. And think of the family. Your grandfather drove a bus for thirty years without one accident. People in this building trust our name."
Ojas was quiet. "So what, I wait two years?"
"Two years. Then I'll sit with you for every lesson."
Ojas sighed. "Fine. But I'm choosing the music."

qa.q: How long did Ojas's grandfather drive a bus without an accident?
qa.a: Thirty years.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he shrugged?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, dismissing the risk because he wanted to drive now.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that helped Ojas accept the rule?
qa.a: She explained the law, the real risk to others and the family's reputation, and offered to help him learn later.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Ojas's final "Fine"?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and glad he accepted the rule, even grudgingly.

grounding: A mother explains to her sixteen-year-old son why he must follow the driving-age law, for safety and the family's good name.

passage:
The first time I saw my Dadaji cry was when he voted after his cataract surgery. He held my arm the whole way to the booth and said, "Seventy years I've never missed it."
I'm Elizabeth, and until that day I thought elections were loud and boring. After it, I started paying attention. I read our civics chapter properly. I asked Pradeep, who is doing law entrance prep, why some laws exist.
Our family has a saying: "We don't embarrass the name." I used to think it just meant don't fail exams. Now I think it's also about how you behave in public, like not jumping queues and not throwing wrappers.
I'm too young to vote. But I've already registered to help at the booth as a volunteer when I'm allowed.

qa.q: What did Dadaji say on the way to the booth?
qa.a: "Seventy years I've never missed it."

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel seeing Dadaji cry at the booth?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt moved and full of admiration, and started taking elections seriously.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth's school do to build on this interest?
qa.a: It could run a mock election or invite a local official to explain how voting and laws work.

qa.q: How might Dadaji feel about Elizabeth's new interest?
qa.a: Dadaji would likely feel proud and happy that his habit has passed to his grandchild.

grounding: A teen reflects on growing civic respect and what family honour means in public life.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10-A, civics project
For the unit on local government, Joseph and Nazia chose to track how complaints reach the municipal office. They filed a real complaint about a broken streetlight near school and followed it.
Joseph was frustrated when nothing happened for two weeks. He wanted to post angry comments online. Nazia said her father would be upset if the family name appeared in a public fight.
They argued, then chose a middle path: a polite follow-up letter, signed by both families, and a visit to the ward office. The light was fixed in the fourth week.
In their presentation, Joseph said, "I thought respecting rules meant staying quiet. It means using them properly." I have shared their letter as a model with the other sections.

qa.q: What did Joseph and Nazia complain about?
qa.a: A broken streetlight near school.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when nothing happened for two weeks?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, wanting to post angry comments online.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: The polite letter signed by both families and a ward office visit worked, because it used the proper system and respected both families.

qa.q: How might Nazia's father see the way they handled it?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and proud that the complaint was made respectfully without a public fight.

grounding: A teacher records teens balancing civic action with care for family reputation.

passage:
Diary, Sunday night
Big fight with Papa today. Our cousin's wedding is next month, and Papa wants the band to play on the road till midnight. I said there's a noise rule after ten, and I read it's the law.
He said, "The whole family will laugh at us if the baraat is quiet."
I said, "And the whole building will hate us if it's loud. That's also family name."
Pankaj bhaiya backed me, which never happens.
Papa went quiet. Then he said he'd ask the police station what time is allowed. I felt proud and also bad for arguing in front of Mummy.
I don't think respecting family and respecting rules have to fight. I just need to find the words better next time.
Aditi

qa.q: Who backed Aditi in the argument?
qa.a: Pankaj bhaiya.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel after Papa agreed to ask the police station?
qa.a: Aditi felt proud but also guilty about arguing in front of Mummy.

qa.q: What could Aditi try next time a family plan and a rule clash?
qa.a: Aditi could raise it early and calmly, bringing the rule and suggesting a solution that keeps the family's pride too.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Aditi called the building's view "family name" too?
qa.a: Papa may have felt caught off guard and a bit challenged, which is why he went quiet before agreeing to check.

grounding: A teen's diary weighing family honour against a public law and finding a respectful path.
